title: Slab-built rectangular soap dish
subtitle: A flat-based dish with raised drainage ribs, built from two rolled slabs
excerpt: This soap dish is built from a flat base slab with a series of raised clay ribs pressed across the bottom to lift the soap and allow water to drain away. A low rim runs around the sides and ends. The piece is made from air-dry clay and sealed inside to manage the damp environment of a bathroom shelf or kitchen sink.
sourceNotes: Slab-built dish technique derived from first principles. Drainage-rib design adapted from traditional ceramic soap dish construction documented in nineteenth-century domestic pottery records.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to even thickness, usually between two wooden guide rails.
The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still damp enough to join and trim.

content.text: A soap dish is a practical first slab project. The form is flat and rectangular: no curves to hold or joins to coax into shape. The drainage ribs, a series of clay strips pressed across the base, lift the soap so air can circulate and the soap does not sit in standing water. Made from air-dry clay and sealed thoroughly, the dish will tolerate the daily moisture of a soap bar even though it cannot be fired.
What you'll need

Around 300 g of air-dry clay. Two 6 mm guide rails for rolling. A card template: base rectangle 11 × 8 cm; four side walls each 1 cm tall (two pieces 11 × 1 cm, two pieces 8 × 1 cm); five drainage rib strips 8 cm long and 5 mm square in section.
Building the dish
Roll a
slab
to 6 mm thickness between the guide rails. Cut the base rectangle 11 × 8 cm. Keep the remaining slab covered.

From the remaining slab, cut four wall strips: two at 11 × 1 cm (the long sides) and two at 8 × 1 cm (the short ends). Also roll five thin coils each 8 cm long and 5 mm in diameter: these are the drainage ribs.
Leave all pieces covered with cling film for 20 minutes to stiffen to
leather-hard
Mix a small cup of
slurry

. Score the underside of each drainage rib and the base surface where each rib will sit. Space five ribs evenly across the base, running parallel to the short ends. Apply slurry to both scored surfaces and press each rib down firmly. The ribs sit upright: 5 mm square, like small walls across the floor of the dish.

Score and slurry the long edges of the base and the bottom of the two long wall strips. Press the long walls along each long edge, holding them vertical until the slurry begins to grip. Support with rolled paper on the outside if needed.
Score and slurry the short ends of the base and the inside faces of the short wall ends. Press the short walls into the corners. Blend the interior corner joints with the wooden rib.
Trim any overhanging wall clay flush with the base using the fettling knife. Smooth all outer corners by dampening a fingertip and running it along each edge.
Drying

Dry the dish flat on a smooth tile at room temperature. The form is small and the walls are thin: it dries in 24 to 36 hours. Check the drainage ribs have not separated from the base during drying by pressing gently; they should feel solid. If a rib has lifted, dampen the join with slurry and press back into place before the piece is fully dry.
Finishing

Sand any rough edges with 240-grit sandpaper. Apply three coats of acrylic sealant to the entire dish: interior base, walls, drainage ribs, and exterior. The extra coat on this project compared to a purely decorative piece compensates for the damp environment. Allow each coat to dry fully before the next. A fourth coat on the base and inside walls is worthwhile if the dish will sit in a wet sink area.
Care

Remove the soap from the dish weekly and rinse the dish under a tap, letting it dry fully between uses. The sealed clay will tolerate this use pattern for many months. If the sealant surface begins to look dull or water soaks into the clay rather than beading off, re-seal with two more coats. Do not leave the dish submerged in water.
Variations

A soap dish is a good first slab project. The shape is flat. There are no curves and no tricky joins. The ribs are clay strips pressed across the base. They lift the soap so air can get under it. The soap does not sit in water. This dish uses air-dry clay. It cannot be fired. Seal it well and it will cope with daily damp from a bar of soap.
Make the walls taller (3 cm) to create a deeper catch tray that holds more drainage water between empties.
Make in paper-clay-air-dry for a lighter, stronger piece with more resistance to edge chipping.

rows.problem: Wall strips pull away from the base at the corners during drying
rows.cause: Insufficient slurry at the join; wall strips drier than the base when joined
rows.fix: Join all pieces at the same moisture level. Score deeply and apply slurry generously to both surfaces. Reinforce the interior corners by pressing a thin coil of soft clay into each corner and blending it with a wooden rib.

rows.problem: Drainage ribs topple over during drying
rows.cause: Ribs attached before the base reached leather-hard; ribs too narrow to stand unsupported
rows.fix: Wait for the base to reach leather-hard before attaching ribs. Widen the rib cross-section to at least 6 × 6 mm so the rib is stable without support.

rows.problem: Base warps into a slight bow during drying
rows.cause: One surface dried faster than the other
rows.fix: Dry on a plaster bat which absorbs moisture from the underside, equalising the drying rate. If warping occurs before fully dry, flip the dish upside down for the last drying stage.
